name: Maitake mushroom (Grifola frondosa)
short: Case report (title only): raised INR with maitake extract plus warfarin. Small cancer and MDS trials: eosinophilia in 4 patients, withdrawals for nausea, joint swelling, rash and itching.
text: A published case report, available on PubMed only as a title without an abstract, is titled "INR elevation with maitake extract in combination with warfarin"; no further details were available, and it is the only interaction named in the cited sources. In a phase I/II dose-escalation trial in 34 postmenopausal women treated for breast cancer, a maitake polysaccharide extract taken by mouth for 3 weeks caused no dose-limiting toxicity, but two patients withdrew because of mild side effects judged possibly related (nausea and joint swelling in one, rash and itching in the other); the extract both raised and lowered different immune measures, and the authors cautioned that botanical agents may depress as well as enhance immune function. In a phase II study of a maitake extract taken by mouth for 12 weeks by people with myelodysplastic syndromes (21 enrolled, 18 evaluable), asymptomatic eosinophilia (raised eosinophil white cells) occurred in 4 patients, and the extract was reported as well tolerated. In an 18-week randomised trial in 47 healthy older Japanese adults eating bread containing maitake mushroom, no participant stopped because of adverse effects. A 2009 systematic review found a lack of systematic study of maitake's safety in humans.
